utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Perhaps the Usher could already find the witness. Would you please verify whether we're in closed session when we -- when you enter the courtroom. Yesterday, we briefly discussed the handwritten letter. Mr. Jordash, I think you still wanted to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We read it, and we do not see a purpose in tendering it. But if the Prosecution wish to have it tendered, we won't oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any reason why you would want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's been referred to now in the testimony. I will ask additional questions about it, so I believe it's appropriate that it would be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, then -- you received a copy. Have you up-loaded a copy in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe we have, but I can look after that, Your Honour, during the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness JF-26. It's appreciated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's appreciated that you're present in court. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony; that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go straight, please, to 1D1642. I want to pick up on where we left yesterday. Page 85 in the e-court, and it's page 105 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: While that's being found: We're returning to the subject of Bogdanovic, Mr. Witness. And on the English, line -- this is your interview, Mr. Witness, from the 17th of February, 2002, your interview you gave to the Prosecution. Do you recall this, or at least --

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you can see there, at line 6 of the English, at least, when -- the question is asked: "When you say he represented state security, do you mean state security of Bosnia or state security of Serbia? "A. Serbia. "Q. Do you personally believe that he was a member of the state security from Serbia? "A. I don't think so. I think that was a group gathered around Radno Bogdanovic. That was a sort of parallel state security. I don't know how to call it, whether patriots or professional intelligence men. You see a man with a secondary school education had such contacts that he could -- that he could easily pick up a phone and call somebody in Serbia and a track with ammunitions, with armament arrives, or uniforms arrive, or he engages the unit of JNA of special forces that attacked Divic and Kula Grad." That's the point I was getting at yesterday. Your use of the term "parallel state security" gathered around Bogdanovic, could you elaborate on that a bit, please?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I roughly said was that my assessment was that this was a parallel state security. Now, whether they called themselves patriots at the time or whatever, but they did use the authority that they had earlier on, and they knew people from earlier on from the MUP and the Ministry of Defence. And it is a well-known thing that the Ministry of Defence is linked with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you mentioned yesterday about Bogdanovic, that prior to his involvement with the Serbian MUP, was involved with the minister of defence. Can you confirm that he was the Serbian assistant minister of defence prior to being the minister of interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is that something you heard when you were involved with visiting Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you visited Bogdanovic, did he recall or mention to you any of his previous contacts with the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing specific was stated, but I know that he worked at the Ministry of Defence, and I know that he knew all of those people who stayed on after he had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many times do you think you visited Bogdanovic; you, personally?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure about two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did I understand you correctly, that you visited with Kostic at some point?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were there discussions during that time about what assistance Bogdanovic could give towards Zvornik and the Serbs in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. For the most part, it boiled down to those reserves of weapons they had in the Republic of the Serb Krajina and reliance on the Ministry of Defence that had links with the JNA, and in this way, Serb military conscripts were recruited in the reserve force of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned -- and we'll come back to Kostic in more depth in a moment or two, but you mentioned in your statement that at some point he told you that his superior's name was Tepavcevic. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the last name, but this may be 1995 or 1994 when he told me that he worked in the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right, and that's what I'm trying to aim at. There wasn't, was there, a discussion during the visit to Bogdanovic, when Kostic was there, a discussion about how Tepavcevic or anyone in the DB could assist? The discussion was about Bogdanovic saying, Well, the army will assist; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Tepavcevic was not mentioned then. The army, the Ministry of Defence, and the Republic of the Serb Krajina was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Kostic didn't speak to you in 1991 or 1992 about how his contacts in the DB would assist?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not mention it at the time. He was simply speaking from the position that he held in the Republic of the Serb Krajina. That's how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you mention in your statement about -- perhaps I can take you there so we can orientate ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 5865, please. I want to stay with the subject of arming. And paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What statement is that? What exhibit number is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say what statement it is, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. It's the statement of the 15th and 16th of December, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's paragraph 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And before that comes up, let me ask you this question: Am I correct that there were several bridges across the Drina at the time of the arming?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There was one bridge at Karakaj; yes?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And there was also an old bridge close by?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This was a bridge -- at least one of those bridges was the way in which the individual volunteers crossed into Zvornik from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it also the way in which some of the weapons which were coming from the JNA were transported into the Zvornik region?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, looking at paragraph 32, if you just read that, you speak of some weapons being illegally obtained from Serbia and Croatia, and you testify there that Branko Grujic told you that he had agreed with some people from the Serbian State Security that they would transfer weapons across the Drina. And am I correct that that transfer took place not over the bridges, but by boat?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the transfer took place by boat. But I said Serbian Security Services, that's what I said. That is what is written there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right, you did make that comment, and that's what is written there, according to what you said before, according to the original. But that transfer took place by boat and not across the bridges. Does that indicate -- or did that indicate to you that that was being done in such a way as to keep it quiet from the authorities who were manning the bridges?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not take part in that transfer, but certainly there is something illegal as concerns this transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, could you think of any other reason why it would be done by boat rather than straight across the bridges?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there was something unofficial about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's return to the subject of Rade Kostic. Is it correct that in February of 1992, or thereabouts, Kostic occupied the position of interior -- minister of the interior of the RSK, assistant, effectively, to Matic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the region of Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from your observations of him and Pavlovic, could this explain why Pavlovic referred to Kostic as "boss" on occasion?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously Kostic was a person of authority for him, and Pavlovic addressed him as "boss" several times in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You have testified about Kostic's involvement with arming or obtaining arms. Was Kostic's involvement with obtaining arms limited to what he arranged or what was arranged through Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned -- no, let me start that again. Is it correct that Kostic had contacts with Dragan Suka or Drago Suka?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Kostic hails from Zvornik, Mali Zvornik, actually, and when he came to the area it is possible that he had some contacts. But I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you just explain who Drago Suka was, what you know about him, please.

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I worked for the police in Zvornik, and Loznica and Mali Zvornik are neighbouring municipalities, and I note that at the time we were working there, we were working in the same state. We were colleagues, we cooperated. I met Drago Suka for the first time when a murder was being investigated that had occurred in Banja Koviljaca. At the time, he worked in this detachment of the State Security - that was the word that was used - for municipality of Loznica or for this region consisting of several municipalities. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 45 of 65 ter 5865.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could I first seek a clarification of one of the previous answers. Witness 26, you said that Kostic's involvement with obtaining arms was limited to what he arranged or what was arranged through Bogdanovic. In your statement, paragraph 37, you say that you knew Rade Kostic personally, but that he did not tell you any details about his position, and that it was after he had died that you became aware of him having known persons because they attended his funeral. Now, what is it that you can positively claim that his involvement didn't go any further, where at the same time you tell us that Kostic did not always discuss details of his position with you, and that you apparently were not even aware of it until after he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we finished the arming in April, when the war started, in 1992. Up until then, I also visited his home, et cetera. The man was working in Slavonia and Baranja. After that, we saw each other a few times. It was always private encounters. I never went to his office. We always visited each other at home. I did not even know that the man worked in the MUP of Serbia and that he was some kind of a - how should I put this? - person of importance until I went to attend his funeral. And everything that I'm saying is confirmed in my statement as well. Everything actually corresponds to this story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not saying that that is inconsistent. What I'm asking you is that where, apparently at a certain moment, he, although being a personal friend, he did not share certain information with you, why you exclude for the possibility that his role in arming may have gone beyond what he shared with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, in April of 1992, that was when the conflict started. We had armed by then, and by that point JNA or VRS had no need for either Slavonia, or Baranja, or any additional arming. We had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 45, just have a look at that, Mr. Witness, please. Could I ask you this: Is it fair to say that you don't have any evidence to back up what you heard about the involvement of Dragan Suka with Pavlovic concerning weapon distribution? You didn't see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a rather peculiar question. I have to explain this. We were still one state. I lived in the municipality of Mali Zvornik. My house and that of the chief of police of Mali Zvornik were next to each other. There was a yard between us. We were on visiting terms. Suka and Pavlovic would come to visit both him and me. Now, in answer to the Prosecutor's question whether Marko Pavlovic was on visiting terms with Suka, my answer was, yes, because we were all on visiting terms. Since this is a small town, we were socialising. But I have no direct knowledge as to what sort of a relationship he had with Suka, whether there was a professional aspect to it or not. I know that privately they were on visiting terms, just as Goran Zugic would drop by at that time, as well as all the other individuals who were part of that company. There was Mustafic with us as well, and Fadil Mujic, the entire crowd. We would be seeing each other in the home of the chief of the police of Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have on the screen, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding: What Mr. Jordash asked you is whether, apart from hearing about these matters, whether you have any other evidence. Did I understand your answer well that what you heard, you heard that from Pavlovic and Suka, and perhaps others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I know is that Pavlovic and Suka were together in my company on a couple of occasions. Now, what the nature of their relationship was, what they were up to together, is not something I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in your statement, it reads: "I heard they did a lot of work to organise weapons distribution." Did you hear that from Pavlovic and Suka or did you hear that from anyone else? And if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this was a comment by Vidovic, or I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Vidovic, the commander of the police station in Mali Zvornik. Are these the matters that were discussed when you socialised with Vidovic and the others you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We would frequently discuss activities, but I don't know what the true nature of the relationship between Suka and the other individuals was. All of us avoided the subject. So as soon as Suka would be part of the company, we wouldn't be that open and frank in our conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, your statement says that it is as vague as that they did a lot of work to organise weapon distribution, and that is -- although you did not thoroughly discuss the matters, that's what you learned during those conversations; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we may have had suspicions about the nature of the relationship between Pavlovic and Suka, and I don't know if they had any sort of special relationship. What I focused on was whether they socialised. And I did say that I saw them together, but I don't know the nature of their relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in your statement, you go further, isn't it, and even in one of your previous answers you told us that this was Vidovic's comment. Now you suddenly step back and say that you had suspicions. Well, even not knowing whether what was said was true or not, I'm focusing exclusively on what you heard at the time, and which is in your statement described that you heard they did a lot of work to organise weapon distribution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's accurately written, but I think that, as a matter of fact, Drago Suka would be part of the company in order to see what Marko Pavlovic was up to. He wasn't quite clear on what he was doing, and I think that the point of him socialising in our company was to find out what Marko Pavlovic's role and activities were. I think that officially he was monitoring him. He was, in fact, trying to gather, I think, intelligence about who he was and what he was doing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, you say it's accurate that you heard that they did a lot of work to organise weapon distribution, which is a bit different from the one monitoring the other, isn't it, trying to find intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say that, but it's not true, Judge. I said it inadvertently, but it's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is not true, the monitoring or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any information to the effect that Drago Suka worked together with Marko Pavlovic. I think that Drago Suka monitored Pavlovic as a person of interest who appeared in Mali Zvornik, Zvornik, Tuzla, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But where you said that this is accurately written, you confirm that you said that you heard that they did a lot of work to organise weapon distribution. But now you say, although you have said it, it's not true. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a look also at the video underlying the statement in this respect. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D162 is admitted into evidence, under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we have, please, Rule 65 ter 4655. And this is a State Security Department official note again, this time dated 7th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we see there Radoslav Kostic's name?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So 7th of January, 1992, very shortly before the critical events in Zvornik, Kostic appears to be providing information to the State Security Department of Serbia. And my question is: Did you ever find out from Kostic or have any indication from Kostic concerning his precise obligations towards the State Security Department in Serbia, vis-a-vis providing information as an operative?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our socialising was of a private nature. He didn't tell me much about his official contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. For Your Honours' information, it's accepted from the Stanisic Defence that Kostic had these obligations towards the State Security and was employed in that role at this period in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to assist in providing some background information concerning police officers of Serb nationality in the RSK in this way: Am I correct that towards the end of 1990 and in 1991, many police officers of Serb nationality were expelled from the various -- or various SUPs within the RSK region, expelled by Croats?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you privy to any information concerning what happened to many of those hundreds of police officers, in terms of their applying, then, to the Serb service for some form of employment so that they could sustain themselves and provide a livelihood for themselves?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the then Yugoslavia had not yet recognised the secession of Slovenia and Croatia, it was the obligation of the SUP to receive all those who wanted to move on to Serbia, because these were policemen, they didn't know what else to do. It was their livelihood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so many of these hundreds of police officers were then employed or at least received a stipend from the Serbian MUP; are you privy to that information?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even today I know dozens of such individuals who had precisely that shift of -- in their career. That was standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And a few, a very few, I suggest, such as Kostic, were employed on an operative basis within the Serbian DB, with the majority of these police officers being assigned to the public security?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In your dealings with Kostic, did you -- let me start that again. In your dealings with Kostic, did he ever tell you that prior to being fired from his position as the police station commander in Darda, he had been a candidate for the assistant minister of the interior in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Basically, he was considered to be an excellent police officer, and that's why he was a candidate for the assistant minister of the interior in Zagreb; did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I stayed there in that town, and he was considered the best policeman, a person of authority, and excelled in every sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest that Kostic was known to be an honest and a decent man. That was his reputation within Darda and the outlying regions of Darda?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about Kostic warning you not to communicate with Arkan, and I want to understand that a little more, because I'm going to suggest that Kostic, even prior to becoming assistant to Martic, was against a movement of paramilitaries into -- in Eastern Slavonia and into the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was in Bijeljina, Arkan set up his structure there. He would always bring along a couple of his men and would then have some locals join. He would have this organisation there, and then he would move on -- and he moved on to Zvornik. I was 26 when the conflict broke out. However, fortunately, I saw Kostic in that period of time, told him of this whole idea, and he, in turn, told me that these were problematic people who had problematic records, and that I should, by no means, have any contacts with them, that I should try to avoid any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness also said something about the contact between him and Arkan, and that's not reflected in the record. And I'm referring to this last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you say anything about your contacts with Arkan, and could you please repeat that, Witness JF-026?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't understand English. I don't know what was interpreted. But the gist of it is that Arkan suggested that he should have the Serbian Volunteer Guard present in Zvornik. And me, being a young man, found it interesting, found it appealing. He offered that I should be the leader of that field structure of his, but, fortunately, several days later I saw Kostic. We had a private conversation, where I shared this idea with him, and he replied that I should not be in contact with these people, that I should refuse this, that I should not have any contacts with people that he considered problematic, and that I should avoid any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have, please, on the screen D67. Not to be shown to the public. Thank you. This is another State Security report, 7th of January, 1992. Could we go, please, to -- I'm not interested, particularly, in the author of this at the moment. But if we look at page 7 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S, I want to ask about a particular man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You see the second paragraph there concerning: "Unconfirmed reports indicate that Zeljko Raznatovic, aka Arkan, has founded a so-called Serbian Volunteer Guard ..." If you just read that paragraph to the end to yourself, I'll ask you a question or two about it. Now, have you read that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if this man, Djordje Bozovic, aka Giska, did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you hear about him and he being the commander of a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I know it's long time ago to remember conversations, but I suggest that Kostic was responsible for threatening Giska in Eastern Slavonia and ordering him to leave Eastern Slavonia, and successfully removing his group from Eastern Slavonia. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he wanted to protect his family, because apparently there had been some threats, and that apparently Giska was involved. So he was trying to get his family out of harm's way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the threat involved Kostic basically pulling a gun on Giska and ordering him and his group of approximately 30 men to leave Eastern Slavonia. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely why he was threatened by that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The last answer is still puzzling me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've just given an answer which says: "Yes. That is precisely why he was threatened by that group." Who was threatened by that group?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Kostic took part in throwing that group of volunteers out. I think it had been organised by some political party from Belgrade. They were like a paramilitary structure. He threw them out. And I know that he told me that he was careful about where his children were moving about, because he had received threats on account of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Threats on account of what?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of this group of Giska's, because he expelled them from Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the sequence of events is: Kostic throws out this -- or takes part in removing this paramilitary group. As a result of that, they threaten his family?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to just return very briefly to Bogdanovic. Did Bogdanovic not mention at any stage his contacts with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in front of me. But it's a well-known thing that he was president of the Red Star Football Club and Arkan was leader of the fans there, so I think that that contact and relationship is from those days. And how it developed further, I don't know. Also, rumour had it that when Arkan was arrested in Zagreb by the Croatian police, that Bogdanovic phoned the then minister of the interior to release him. To everyone's surprise, he released him within two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This was towards the end of 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before the start of the conflict in Croatia. Or, actually, the clashes had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at that point, Bogdanovic was the minister of interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was it well known or well rumoured that Arkan had received his weapons from the federal institute at that time which was a part of the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said here that he came then in a car that had license plates that belonged to the federal SUP and with full police gear; I mean, uniform, weapons, and communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to try to understand what happened concerning Arkan's arrival in Zvornik. You first saw Arkan in Bijeljina or Zvornik; which one?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you speak to him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him what the situation was like in Zvornik, and I extended an invitation to him, on behalf of the Crisis Staff, to come to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So at that point in time when you extended the invitation -- well, why did you extend the invitation at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because conflicts had broken out in Zvornik, the JNA was attacked by the Muslims, we were a minority, we were expelled from Zvornik. Quite simply, I mean, at the time we were in an unenviable position, and we sought help.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So at that point, it was your understanding that Arkan had not decided or been asked to come to Zvornik; he was then engaged in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed [as interpreted] in Bijeljina at the time, and I went there with my assistant, who was officially on the police force, because we were sent by the Crisis Staff to invite him. Had we known that he would be coming, we would not go there to ask him to come. After all, as we crossed the Drina and -- I mean, the way we crossed the Drina and where we stayed, that shows that there was no preconceived organisation. It is simply that the situation was such that different decisions had to be made from one minute to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean, the way you crossed the Drina indicated that there was no preconceived organisation?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Bosnia there were already barricades, roadblocks, in all urban areas. Near the village of Badovinci, we crossed the Drina on a small boat, not across the bridge, and then during the night we went towards Zvornik. And since we had nowhere to put them up in Zvornik, because the Muslims held the town itself, we put them up only for one night in a remote hotel that is called Radalj. This is about six or seven kilometres away from the border with Bosnia. The Crisis Staff paid for their accommodation at that hotel. Quite simply, they were guests of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, perhaps I'm a bit confused. One of your answers started: "He was killed in Bijeljina at the time ..." Who were you referring to? Perhaps the -- my colleague suggests that there may be a transcript or translation error and that he was still in Bijeljina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that must be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's caused my confusion. Now, you said you went there. You were sent by the Crisis Staff to invite him. In your statement, we read that Rade Kostic phoned you and told you that you were to go to Bijeljina. Is that the same trip you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has to do with the same trip. In the statement, I did say that we called that Parliamentary Committee for Serbs Outside Serbia. We asked different people for help. Inter alia, we spoke to Kostic, who was in Darda at the time. However, since Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you're talking about the same trip. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your statement, it reads: "Arkan told me that the next goal of his unit was Zvornik, and he asked about the situation in Zvornik. My impression was that it had all been arranged or co-ordinated. Biljana Plavsic said so, and Rade Kostic told us this as well." Is that correct, or is correct what you told us, or could you explain how to understand the statement compared to the answers you've just given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would really like to explain this to you, Judge. It is correct that we contacted the ministry -- or, rather, this committee, this parliamentary committee. We called Sarajevo, we called the headquarters of the SDS, we called the Crisis Staff that was at the level of Republika Srpska. We called everyone. We were looking for anybody's help, and, inter alia, we spoke to Kostic. It is true that I went, at that proposal of the Crisis Staff, with my assistant to invite Arkan, because there was this very similar situation that had occurred in Bijeljina and he resolved it within two days. In Bijeljina, also, the Muslims took the town first, and then Arkan came with his unit and established Serb authority in Bijeljina. The same thing happened in Zvornik. It is correct that he said to me that he had heard that that had happened in Zvornik and that his next destination is Zvornik. I don't know where else he went afterwards, in terms of the theatre of war, but I believed then that there was some plan, that the federal SUP or the federal state, that at the time did not recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina, did have some sort of plan to resolve the crisis. We particularly believed in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the meeting you talked about which took only two minutes; is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the Cultural Centre in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps it's me, but I don't understand what the role of Kostic was in this.

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, we called 50 different sources of assistance. We were asking for help. He was in Darda. We asked whether he had any weapons left and whether he had any possibility to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And he informed you what concerning Arkan?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we were talking, we referred to how the situation had been resolved in Bijeljina. Although his view of Arkan was highly negative, he did say at that point in time, You see how they resolve things in Bijeljina. You could do the same thing. And that was a signal for me to go and call Arkan and his people, because, after all, Bijeljina had a different population structure that was far more favourable to the Serbs than Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that conversation took place when?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'm not sure about the date, but it may be the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that was Kostic's involvement, limited to that suggestion, involvement with Arkan's arrival in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Jordash, I'd like, then, to seek clarification of the statement. Witness JF-026, you said, in relation to going to Arkan: "My impression was that it had all been arranged or co-ordinated. Biljana Plavsic said so, and Rade Kostic told us this as well." So apparently there are now two versions of the story. The one is Kostic, one out of fifty people you approached, Kostic saying, Well, perhaps you could ask Arkan, who did something in Bijeljina, it might assist you as well. And the other one, the other version of the story is Kostic telling you, Report to Arkan, you have a two or three minutes' conversation with him, and you are told by Biljana Plavsic and by Kostic that all had been prearranged and that Arkan had already on his mind to come to Zvornik anyhow. Now, explain to us what is the most -- what's the version which comes closest to the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, the closest thing to the truth is that they were saying to us, Don't worry, everything is organised. Don't worry, wait for the JNA. There is the federal state. Bosnia is not going to be recognised as an independent state, and

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, it was -- yes, the second version, therefore, is closer to the truth. You got the impression that when you were sent to report to Arkan and when you had this very brief conversation, that matters had been arranged already and that you didn't have to bother about it; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, that is the way it was, roughly. Well, we wouldn't have gone to get him and to ask him to come if we had known that he would be coming. Also, there's another thing. Different communities in Bosnia fared on the basis of the organisation they actually had. Some fared better, others fared worse. I don't know how to explain this to you. Our arrangement was aimed at preserving the former state, Yugoslavia. We believed that the JNA and the federal SUP would lead the effort. At that time, a colonel general headed the federal Ministry of the Interior, Petar Gracanin. We believed that that situation would be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now going into details I, at least, did not ask for. Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock. We're well beyond 75 minutes. As far as your assessment is concerned, the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I could have another 30 minutes, that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another 30 minutes. Yes. I'm not informed about any arrangements -- travel arrangements made or whether that matter has been resolved or not. I don't know whether you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've been informed that, unfortunately, because of the adverse weather condition, the usual indirect flights are not flying. So apart from a 1.00 flight, which is direct, I'm afraid the witness is a bit stuck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the snow, rather, at this moment than the Tribunal. We have a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11. And then you have another 30 minutes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I allow you to continue, Mr. Jordash: Yesterday, you'll find on the record that the status of D157 was changed into public. That is a mistake. It was about D158. That was the one which was provisionally admitted confidentially, and that's the document, D158, which then changed its status. This being corrected, you may proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to pick up very quickly, Mr. Witness, on the issue of Arkan and any plan. Now, you've told us about Arkan turning up with federal MUP plates. Was there an assumption at the time on that basis, amongst you and other members of the authorities in Zvornik, that Arkan had been sent by authorities in the federal MUP?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was the federal minister of interior Petar Gracanin at that moment in time?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you hear also around that time that Petar Gracanin had contacted Mico Stanisic, minister of interior of Republika Srpska, offering the federal MUP's assistance in East Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you hear about Gracanin sending a different federal MUP unit to Sarajevo, commanded by Chief -- commanded by Mico Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mico Davidovic. He is from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if he was sent by Gracanin to command a federal MUP unit in Sarajevo in and around the time of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Gracanin's name mentioned ever in relation to Arkan's arrival in Zvornik, or Bijeljina, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just mentioned the federal SUP, but no one asked who the minister was at the time and who was the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave the matter there. Now, just dealing with, I think, two last subjects: One, JNA participation in the attack on Zvornik, and then I want to deal with Stanisic after that. Am I correct that immediately prior to the clash in Zvornik on the 8th, there was a meeting in Hotel Jezero involving Marko Pavlovic and members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the meeting involved General Savo Jankovic, commander of the Tuzla Corps, and various officers, including Tacic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Tacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what was discussed at that meeting immediately prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what was discussed was resolving the situation in Zvornik that was being held by the Muslims, and what was discussed was how to get it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How to get what back?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, how to restore Serb authority in Zvornik. It was the SDS and the SDA that were in a coalition at the time, actually, so we had been in government together. And then they took over, and then we Serbs organised ourselves and took over from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So this was ostensibly a meeting about the military take-over of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to refer, Your Honours, to 101694. Please, could we have that in e-court. It's an excerpt from a Prosecution expert report in the Perisic case. It's the Butler report, 1D1695. Sorry, I gave you the wrong code. And it's page 161 of e-court. Page 6 of the actual report, but I think if we focus on 161 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't think you're going to be able to read this, unfortunately, Mr. Witness, but I'll read it to you. Paragraph 1.3 there, Mr. Butler's expert opinion is as follows: "With respect to the town of Zvornik, the conflict erupted in the early evening hours of 8th of April, 1992, when elements of the JNA 336th Motorised Brigade, Arkan's Serbian Volunteer Guards, and local SDS-backed TO units seized control of the predominantly Muslim-populated town." Do you disagree with anything in that sentence, Mr. Witness? I can read it to you again, if you need me to.

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That these three elements took part in the conflict on the 8th of April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then the next sentence reads: "This attack was preceded by an ultimatum issued several hours earlier to Zvornik SDA representatives at the Hotel Jezero in Mali Zvornik." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then moving to the next page: "As reflected in a message sent by SDA representative Izet Mehinagic to both General-Major Savo Jankovic, the JNA 17th Corps commander, and Colonel-General Kukanjac, the commander of the 2nd Military District, Arkan and local SDS officials demanded the surrender of the town." Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you confirm this expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was present when Arkan called Osman Mustafic, the chief of police, and told him as much. And then in Hotel Jezero, he slapped about some individuals who were present there in order to intimidate the head of the municipality, who was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... and another individual who was also a Muslim whose name I now forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the first name of the Muslim? The interpreters did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president of the municipality of Zvornik, Abdulah Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the paragraph goes on to say: "Also noted present at this meeting was JNA Captain Dragan Obrenovic, then commanding a battalion of the 336th Motorised Brigade garrisoned in and around Zvornik." Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen 1D1700. This is a witness who testified in the Seselj case in open conditions, a man called Asim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I take it that you're following the usual procedure that if a witness -- if the statement or testimony of another witness is put to this witness, that you first ask questions about what he knows about it; only then. But it may be that it's a matter already dealt with. I do not know, but I just remind you of the good practice in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before I ask you, then, about this testimony, I want to take you just immediately before the take-over of Zvornik. Are you aware of events concerning a clash between JNA personnel and Muslim military troops in Sapna?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the police at the time, so I know the event. There was a JNA column passing through that town, and it was attacked, and I think four soldiers were killed and a number wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was it attacked by?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was attacked by the Muslim population. I think that by the time, these were already Green Berets, the formations that they had organised already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And is it correct that this was, effectively, an ambush on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain sense, yes, as an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when did this happen in relation to the 8th of --

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 4th or the 5th of May. I'm sorry, 4th or the 5th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the first place, is it correct that the news that came out of this attack was that four or five JNA soldiers had gone missing?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there a demand for their return?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who made the demand?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know specifically who?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it was the then Captain Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there a threat accompanying that demand?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that Zvornik would be razed to the ground unless they returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were they returned?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of it that was captured was returned, but I think there were four soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the end of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer. You said: "Some of it that was captured was returned, but I think that there were four soldiers ..." And what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several soldiers that were taken prisoner, and they returned. But I think four of them were killed in Sapna. Among them was an officer. I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there then a further demand about the return of the weapons that had been taken during the attack?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did that have anything to do with Colonel Tacic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dragan Obrenovic was in Colonel Tacic's unit, but we had no more contacts with Obrenovic anymore, though he was closer to us. But Tacic was his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So did Tacic then take control or take command of this particular issue, i.e., the return of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Colonel Tacic make any further threats concerning the return of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the conflict, it was obvious that there were serious threats and that a serious conflict was to follow. Then, what followed was the official recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the United Nations, and that was when all the complications started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. So within -- is this right? Within a day or two of Tacic making the threat, the attack on Zvornik started involving the three entities we saw in the report?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, just to complete this: Did Arkan leave Zvornik as a result of anything that Colonel Tacic did? This is after the attack on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it subsequently. At the time, I did not have any personal knowledge. I heard that there was a conflict between them, that they clashed, and that this was the reason why Arkan left. But I did not have any direct knowledge of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What were you told subsequently about the clash and why and how Arkan left?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan was arrogant with the officers. I think that there was slapping about, a tussle. I don't know what the reasons were, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. But is it suffice to say that Colonel Tacic ordered Arkan to leave, and Arkan obeyed?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, picking up on a few smaller subjects: Is it correct that it was well known, during the attack on Zvornik, that Arkan's Men were in conflict with the SRS men?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What makes you believe that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply, Arkan wanted those various groups to be under his control, and he wanted all those volunteer units to be under him, and I think that they resisted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about Dragan and his training centre, Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he had a guest appearance on Radio Zvornik. It happened sometime after my departure from the police in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you hear about his comments concerning having the support of Karadzic and ministers of the RS, Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he was brought over there as an instructor. He gathered individuals from volunteer units and some locals and tried to carry out some sort of training with these men who apparently did not have any war experience. He was there in the capacity of an instructor. He didn't have any units of his own. I think that he was engaged by those from the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska to train people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. A different subject. You know about Vaso Mijovic being accommodated in Bratunac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Vaso Mijovic was stationed in Bratunac. He also had a group of locals with him. There was some sort of clash with the local authorities in Bratunac, so those from the MUP of Republika Srpska dispatched him there as an instructor. I know that he was also slapping about the president of the municipality and of the Executive Board. I went on a private visit to see him, and I brought him some cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it well known, before he arrived, that there was chaos in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was incredible chaos in Bratunac on all levels, so he put together a unit that was billeted in the daycare centre -- in the kindergarten in Bratunac, and he seemingly did introduce some order to it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say "order," what kind of order did he introduce?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was plunder, harassment of the Muslim population, all sorts of criminal acts. The police was feeble, because there was only 10 to 15 Serbian policemen, so he put together a group of locals whom he trained, to a certain extent, and who then tried to restore law and order, as far as the war circumstances would permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what happened to him after he'd done that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I saw him once or twice in private contacts. He went to Montenegro. I know that he hailed from Bratunac. He married a doctor who worked in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So he had no problem in -- let me rephrase that. Did he return then to live in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He left there for a while, but then he moved to Montenegro. So I'm not sure how much time he spent in Bratunac. I know for a fact that he -- his wife was from Bratunac, that he married there, and it was along those lines that he had frequent contacts with Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So frequent -- post his introducing some order to the place, he remained at times and had frequent contacts with civilians there?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have, please, on e-court 65 ter 4800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, in eight minutes from now you will have used thirty-five minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm almost there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is an -- as you can see, a Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Security Services Centre, Bijeljina, 25th of June, 1992, request for equipment to the TO of Serbia. And it notes: "The Zvornik Public Security Station, with an active and reserve complement currently numbering around 500. When equipping our members, we were helped by the Republican Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, which provided both quarter-master supplies and technical equipment. Since they do not have some of the police equipment, we would like to ask and request that you assist in finding equipment and send us, if you are able, the following -- able to, the following supplies and equipment:" And then there's a list: "Armoured combat vehicle. "7.62-millimetre or 7.65-millimetre pistol." And then over the page: "A silencer for sniper and AP/automatic rifle." Are you able to confirm that there was limited supplies provided by the MUP of Serbia to assist the police stations in Zvornik, and it didn't include this type of military hardware?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we split as the Serbian police station in Zvornik, and let me note that still we were a joint state, Yugoslavia, the colleagues from adjacent police stations helped us, as far as they could, though they didn't have much to share. We would receive a couple of uniforms, perhaps. But as for the armoured vehicles, the police station in Zvornik never had those, either before the war or even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I apply to tender this as an exhibit, please, MFI'd if Mr. Groome has objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We ask that this be MFI'd, Your Honour, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D163, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D163 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One very quick last issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In your statement of 2008, you say, at paragraph 91 - I'll try to short-cut things - that you were told by Branko Grujic that he had met at least once with Jovica Stanisic in a restaurant in Mali Zvornik named Planina just before the conflict started. Do you remember that comment?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that's my personal knowledge. Was the intention of Branko Grujic to impress anyone, did he meet with anyone, I don't know. He never told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen 1D1694, which was an interview with Grujic by the Prosecution. And let's go to page 5 of e-court. There isn't, I'm afraid, a B/C/S translation. We go to the bottom of the page. The Prosecution ask Grujic: "Was the DB in Serbia involved in supplying weapons to the Serbs in the municipality of Zvornik?" Over the page: "Not that I know of. "Q. What about the MUP of Serbia, in general. "A. To the best of my knowledge, nobody interfered. It's possible that they did it through some other lines, but not that I know of." And if we go over the page to page 7 in e-court: "Did you meet with any officials from the Serbian DB? "A. I only briefly -- I only met briefly Mr. Jovica Stanisic, then head of the DB, but it was a rather -- very brief encounter, rather than a meeting. And it was later on in 1993, prior to the war, we never met, and it was when the pilots actually hijacked in Pale and when they were supposed to be handed over to the Serb authorities in Serbia. So he was waiting for those pilots to take them over, and this is how we met unofficially at Jezero Hotel."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could it be that that's what Grujic told you?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite possible. Hotel Jezero and Restaurant Planina are 50 metres apart, so it's quite possible that I mixed them up and that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got nothing further. Thank you, Mr. Witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Groome, are you ready to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, you provided the Chamber with a letter you sent to the VWS. One of the issues you raised in that letter was a request for documentation related to the United States or to the European Union. Did you request this documentation because you believed your co-operation with the ICTY entitled you to it or because of security concerns, the concerns you expressed at the start of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I requested that because of the position of my family and myself in the community where I live. I don't know whether you can understand this, but to live in Serbia as a witness who testified in The Hague is practically impossible; if you want to have a normal life, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So can I take from your answer that had you been given such documentation, it was your intention to move from where you now reside?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just check? We have no official translation of the letter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether it is about documentation or because the provisional translation I received, and I just read the last -- and, again, this is not an official translation, reads: "I am kindly asking you to consider the possibility if you could please arrange that my family and I receive citizenship of one of the European Union states or that of the United States of America," which goes beyond documentation. I see Mr. Petrovic is nodding. Is that what you wanted to raise as well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Nowhere here is any documentation mentioned in this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently, therefore, we have no official translation. The request was not, as I understand, about documentation, but about assistance -- arranging for receiving citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, if you had been granted citizenship in either an EU country or the US, was it your intention to move with your family from where you now live?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I ask you to tell us, the business that you've described in passing, can you give us some sense of the number of businesses that you own?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So should we take, from the fact that you contemplated leaving that behind and moving to another country because of your concerns, as a reflection of the gravity or the seriousness which you consider these concerns?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't leave that capital. I would sell everything and transfer it there. That was my intention. But I'm telling you, being a witness in five trials and going on living there, that is impossible. Now, how do I describe this? I'm telling you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question. Now, at several points in your evidence here, you have clarified your previous use of the phrase "Serbian State Security Services" and said that you mention "Serbian Security Services," and we can see the most recent instance of this on today's transcript at page 7. I want to ask you some detailed questions about the organisation you referred to as Serbian Security Services. The first is: Do you know what ministry of the Serbian Government this organisation was within?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to clarify. This does not have to do with clarification --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd prefer if the witness could clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know if there's any problem with the question as put by Mr. Groome. One second --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is, okay. One second. Could you take your earphones off for a second, Witness JF-026. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not the issue of translation -- this is not the issue of clarification. This is the issue of translation. Please take a look at paragraph 32 of his statement, because that is the paragraph which was corrected or clarified this morning and yesterday. The Serbian version, which was read and signed by the witness, says different from the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it, then, in your view, says, because the witness has corrected several times. We have, in paragraph 32, "Serbian State Security," we have in paragraph 37 "State Security Service," and what is -- I think, as a matter of fact, that where the witness has explained that the reference to the Serbian State Security is incorrect and that it should be understood as "State Security Services," that Mr. Groome at this moment is exploring what organisation -- or what, actually, the witness referred to when he talks about "State Security Services." Now, what is wrong in the basis of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is that he didn't correct anything. This was the translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. Then if we then -- perhaps, could you tell me, because I haven't got the original, what does it say in his own language?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In his language, it reads "Serbian Security Services," which differs from "Serbian State Security," as you have in English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the same in both 32 and -- well, in 37, the word "Serbian" doesn't appear, so you would like -- no, 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: 32, that relates only to paragraph 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And you say it's "Serbian Security Services"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the interpreters have most likely found the proper wording of translating that. If you would carefully listen, Mr. Petrovic, that if Mr. Groome uses the words "Serbian Security Services," because I take it, Mr. Groome, that's what you are asking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm happy to discuss translation issues outside of court. It's really -- I just want to get this witness's understanding of that term that he's used several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that point. Mr. Petrovic will carefully listen whether these -- if used in English, "Serbian Security Services," whether the way in which that is translated is the same as what you find in the original B/C/S version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone happy? Please proceed, Mr. Groome. And let me just see the -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, I want to understand what it is you're referring to when you use the phrase "Serbian Security Services." And my first question in this regard is: Do you know what ministry of the Serbian Government this organisation was within?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are several of them. There is the Military Security that is under the Ministry of Defence. Then there is State Security that is within the Ministry of the Interior. Then there is that security that is within the Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if I can be clear, there are three possibilities in your mind: A security service within the military --

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- one with the Foreign Service or Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and one within the Serbian State Security or the Serbian Ministry of Interior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is those three that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, up until very recently, if I'm not mistaken, the Socialist Federal Republic of FRY went from that to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to Serbia and Montenegro. It is really relatively recently that Serbia is standing alone as an independent country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why it was you used or you conceive of the term "Serbian Security Services" as an organisation that could fall within the federal government of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're a professional, you pay attention to every little detail. As far as I'm concerned, there's the Drina, and on the other side, there's Serbia. Sometimes I say "Serb," sometimes I say "Yugoslav." But if we were to speak properly, all the way up to 1992 or 1993, or I don't know, 2000, it would be the Yugoslav services. And from 2000 onwards, the Serb services. However, in my mind, it is the Drina, and on the other bank is Serbia. I didn't really pay attention to these details. I said, correctly, "Serbian Services -- Security Services," but if we are talking about the possibility of arming on the other side of the Drina. However, the right phrase for me to use would be "Yugoslav services," because it was the JNA at the time, there was the weaponry, the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, where was the office of the Crisis Staff in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the Crisis Staff in Zvornik was in the so-called Russian building, Ruska Zgrada. On the ground floor, there was an office. That was the office of the SDS, the Serb Democratic Party. Because we were a new political party and the municipality gave us some offices to use, and we had our office in that Russian building on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we can get you on your way back home quicker if you limit your answers to the specific information I'm asking. Can I ask you to tell us, what was the Alhos factory, and were meetings of the Crisis Staff held there?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now we are speaking about time-limits. We moved out to Karakaj. This Alhos is in Zvornik, and the Crisis Staff had its headquarters in Alhos. It is a textile factory in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Since time is important: During what period did the Crisis Staff have its headquarters in the Alhos factory?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say from the 5th or 6th of April onwards, April and May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could I ask that P1380, marked for identification, be called to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that is being done, sir: Mr. Jordash showed you an expert report by Mr. Butler, in which he put to you a number of the facts asserted in that report, and you gave evidence that you believed them to be correct. One of the facts recorded -- or referred to a letter by Izet Mehinagic, and that is what I'm asking to be called to the screen before us. I ask that we focus on the second paragraph. Now, in the beginning of the second paragraph, the author writes: "Zvornik was given an offer to lay down its arms and the Crisis Staff of the Zvornik SO will make a decision on the ultimatum at 1600 hours." My question to you is: Is this the same ultimatum which you've given evidence about a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let's -- I want to continue reading on. The author writes: "I do not think that the ultimatum will be accepted, and that this will lead to an unprecedented massacre of the unprotected and innocent population and to horrible environmental consequences as a result of suicidal action by the desperate population. I send you this dispatch as a cry to heaven and an appeal to you to act in line with the most illustrious traditions of the JNA and the most sacred moral norms of our peoples and to protect the endangered population from a catastrophe such as they have never experienced in their history." Now, this author makes a specific request of the JNA, General Jankovic, and it's found in the last line of this same paragraph. He says: "The only solution is to deploy your units from the zone in which they now find themselves together with the forces threatening the population and station them at the approaches to the town, where they will defend the endangered population from the oppressors." My question to you is: Do you know if General Jankovic ever re-deployed his troops to prevent Serb volunteers from entering the town and doing what they did?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the JNA entered town together with the volunteers. You see this paragraph down here, that the town remain a Yugoslav town. That was the core of the matter, Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, at transcript page 41, you had the following exchange with Mr. Petrovic: "As far as you're aware, Arkan's Men acted as part of the JNA, in other words, part of the Armed Forces of the SFRY during this period that we're referring to, 1992; isn't that right?" Your answer: "Yes."
