My question is: If during that time it was your belief that Arkan was acting as part of the JNA, can you tell us why it was that you discussed the possibility of Arkan coming to Zvornik with Rade Kostic, who you have heard here today the Defence now admits was a State Security operative, rather than speaking with General Svetozar Andric, who you described yesterday as your contact in the JNA and who had provided roughly 90 per cent of the weapons distributed to local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the witness's testimony is being presented incorrectly. The witness did not only talk to Radoslav Kostic. Today, he said that he talked to tens of persons, so it is an incorrect quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, it's not an incorrect quote. It quotes part of what the witness said. And the question, apparently, is focused on that. Therefore, your intervention was not an accurate one. Mr. Groome started asking about the other 49 -- Mr. Groome is asking about that one, although I tend to agree with you that if we have not identified the other 49, that we do not know who they are, so that -- but that's something the witness might raise or not raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll ask to clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, did you have a conversation with General Andric about the possibility of Arkan coming to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Prosecutor, there is a problem there. We did not know Svetozar Andric at the time at all. Everything seems to be confused here, the entire picture from 1992 to 1995. Svetozar Andric was not in Zvornik at the time at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, simply, was whether you spoke with him. Now, the answer, if you didn't know at the time, the answer simply is, "No," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know someone, you can't have a conversation with him. So, therefore, if you would have just said, "No," that would have answered the question. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at transcript page 36 today, you said, quote, and this is in reference to the relationship with the JNA: "Arkan was arrogant with the officers. I think that there was slapping about." Can you give us your understanding of how this person, who you believed to be part of the JNA, was able to slap about officers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those of a lower rank, and they complained to their superiors. In this way, he also wanted to attain the greatest possible authority among them. Believe me, the way most of them -- they behaved -- the way most of them behaved at the beginning of the war made it a well-deserved thing to have them slapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now change the subject. I want to discuss payments made to paramilitaries and volunteers. I want to remind you of an exchange between yourself and Mr. Petrovic yesterday. This is from transcript page 14: "Q. My question is whether the volunteer units, including Zuca's unit in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik at the time, were financed by the provisional municipal authorities in Zvornik? "A. Yes." My first question is: Do you recall personal knowledge of this fact that the paramilitaries and volunteers were paid by the provisional municipal authorities in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have direct knowledge of them receiving salaries from the provisional municipal authorities in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would these volunteers have been paid up until the time of their arrest in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were they paid after their arrest?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who stayed on in the army, most of them were returned to regular units after the arrest, and they received salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that salary provided by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a time-period when there was no Crisis Staff any longer, but there was the provisional government as the successor of the Crisis Staff, and that government provided the salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the person you have described as Jekic, was he part of the police detail that organised the arrest of the paramilitaries in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, objection. Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, let me just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can rephrase, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're willing to do so, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, what, if any, part did Mr. Jekic play in the arrest of the paramilitaries and volunteers in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that he played any kind of role. He was a scumbag who went around falsely representing himself, cheating people out of their money, and seeking personal promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on cross-examination in the first case, you were asked about duration of the fighting in Zvornik, and I will read the following question and answer to refresh your recollection. And I'm reading from

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Could you tell me, please, how long that battle for Zvornik lasted?" And your answer was: "The actual attack on Zvornik lasted from about 4.00 a.m. until 8.00 a.m., so about four hours." Was the center of the town under Serb control by 8.00 a.m. on the same morning, the 8th of April, the day the attack began?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on the next page of that transcript, you were asked about the number of Serb combatants who were killed, and you stated: "I do not have precise records, but I think the Serbs had three or four dead." Do you affirm that number?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the number of Muslim combatants, you said: "According to what the Civil Defence said later on, I think about 20 persons were buried, whose bodies were found there after the battle." Do you affirm that number?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So are we correct to conclude from your evidence that during the initial taking of control of Zvornik by Serb forces, there were approximately 24 combatants killed over the course of approximately four hours?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the following. After taking control of the town on the morning of 8th of April, 1992, and up until their arrest in June of 1992, what function did these paramilitaries and volunteers perform that justified them being paid by municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of time, they were all mobilised. The army deployed them. Part of them came from a Loznica group and from the reserve police force in Zvornik, but very soon they organised themselves in the following way: They became the main people in town after Arkan and his group left, so they became very arrogant and powerful. They arrested people, including the president of the municipality, Grujic. I know that they arrested even ministers who were going to Belgrade and passing through there. I know that they arrested the minister of information, Ostojic, and that is why they were arrested and accounts were settled with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, in addition to these misdeeds that you're describing now, Mr. Jordash tendered a report about Zuca's unit after you confirmed the events described in it. It has been marked for identification as D159. You testified you were aware of the murder described in the document, in which a knife was thrust into Dr. Vidovic's spine because he sold medical supplies to Muslims. You also recognised the events described in a statement of Dusko Vuckovic, marked for identification as D160, in which he describes killing men and women civilians. Vuckovic goes on in the statement to describe how he questioned Muslim detainees by cutting a man's ear off and nailing it to the wall of the Alhos factory. Can you explain to us: Why did the Crisis Staff continue to pay these men when they were doing things such as you've described and as described in these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: assumption was that by then, they were already stronger than the Crisis Staff, they had a stronger group. The official proposal at the Assembly of -- the Municipal Assembly of Zvornik was that Zvornik should be called "Zucin grad," "Zuca's town." This was an official proposal in May 1992, so you can imagine what things were like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I want to change topics a bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm also looking at the clock. You asked for half an hour. Now, I gave a bit extra to Mr. Jordash, so I would not -- without being over-generous, I'll give you a little bit more as well. But how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I meant to intervene after this morning's events. I think I have a bit more to do. I don't think it's substantially that much, but I would imagine I have at least 20 minutes left, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As matters stand now, will there be any need to put further questions to the witness, in view of what Mr. Groome has --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has not granted yet the 20 minutes, but invites you to continue, and is seeking further information at this moment on other matters which might influence our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move as hastily as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, can I ask you to keep your answers as brief as possible, and in this way, hopefully, we can conclude your evidence here today. Do I understand your evidence over the last few days to be, in general terms, that you feared the possibility of being indicted by this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, objection. It's highly leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I perhaps finish, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may finish the question, and the witness should wait to answer it until I have ruled on the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence over the last few days to be, in general terms, that you feared the possibility of being indicted by this Tribunal, and this fear may have affected the information you provided?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the objection stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The objection does stand. It is leading, and Mr. Groome is trying to impeach his own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, these are two -- of course, impeaching -- impeachment often results in then asking permission to ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply summarising the evidence that I believe is now before us. If I've incorrectly characterised it or summarised it, I'm happy to -- for Mr. Jordash to suggest the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if his evidence so far is presented correctly, it did not have to do only with the indictment being issued against him before this Tribunal. I think he did present some other fears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss this in the presence of the witness. Let me see whether I can phrase your question in such a way that it would meet both your need to find an answer on the question you had on your mind, Mr. Groome, and which would also meet the concerns of the Defence teams. Witness JF-026, in your earlier evidence you referred to accommodating -- that is, to give answers which might be welcomed by those who interviewed you. Did you have any fear that other answers might have a negative impact on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I would be unfair if I said that I didn't fear for my fate. I did, because I am aware of the fact that I was close to these events, and the criteria as to who would be accused and who would not were quite peculiar and odd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether they are peculiar or odd or not, did you fear to be indicted at any moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what moment did you fear to be indicted, and indicted -- being indicted by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was afraid up until the point when it was announced that The Hague would no longer be issuing indictments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was announced a year or two ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, which would mean that when you gave your testimony in the second case, you had no such fears for certain; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because the indicted, who was a lawyer -- the indicted person, who was a lawyer, explained to me that there would no longer be any indictments coming out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did he explain that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he told me at a trial precisely on this subject, and you have it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although the Chamber doesn't have that transcript. Mr. Groome, please proceed. I do not think that this matter has been fully explored, so feel free to further explore the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, JF-026, when you refer to this fear, you repeatedly used the term "we," plural, that you were speaking about more than simply yourself. Now, yesterday Mr. Petrovic asked you the names of the persons you refer to as "we," and you said the following at T-9694: "Those were mostly members of the Crisis Staff in Zvornik; Radic, Grujic, Savic, Ivanovic, and some others who I can't remember at the moment." Now, my question to you is: Do you know if any of the members of the Crisis Staff you named were, in fact, or provided information as witnesses to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that it wasn't quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to repeat your answer. The interpreters didn't quite get the entirety of your answer.

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all the members of the Crisis Staff in Zvornik gave statements for the purposes of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you ever have a discussion with the people you named in which you, quote, "played tactical games"? Did you ever actually discuss with these people tactical games or adjusting the evidence?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. In 1996, officially through the Zvornik Court, we were told who the persons were who The Hague Tribunal found interesting and wanted to have interviews with, and these were some 20 people from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question is actually quite precise. What I'm asking is: Did you ever have a conversation with any of the people that you've named about playing tactical games with investigators from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what "playing tactical games" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used that expression, more or less, yourself; that is, adjusting the evidence to what one would want to hear. Did you discuss those matters, that kind of playing games when being interviewed, with any of the persons of the Crisis Staff of Zvornik you named?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, we discussed it amongst ourselves, but it was not candid, the discussion, because our interests are opposed. Some people got killed, others wanted to downplay their roles, and, of course, it is up to the Prosecutor's Office to establish with whom lies most of the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after you named members of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Petrovic then asked you about two specific people and whether they were part of this group that was trying to put itself in the OTP's, quote, "good books." And the two names he gave you were Goran Zugic and Vojislav Jekic. Now, in paragraph 45 of your statement, you describe Goran Zugic as, quote, "chief of State Security in Tuzla." My question is: Was he also a member of the Crisis Staff in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a member of the Crisis Staff in Zvornik. Neither was Vojo Jekic. We didn't discuss the issue with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you did not have a conversation with either of these men about adjusting evidence that would be given to ICTY investigators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't find them interesting. They were not members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this same Goran Zugic who went on to become an adviser to Mr. Milo Djukanovic, the president of Montenegro, and who died in 2000?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was Goran Zugic, who became adviser for internal matters in the Montenegrin government of Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know how he died?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed in some sort of a show-down, and to this day, it remains unknown what the circumstances of the event were. And there was no indictment issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the other person was Vojislav Jekic, and you've already told us that you did not discuss this matter with him. Do you believe that he was a witness who provided information to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by happenstance, I saw him here when I was a witness. He testified just before me in Case 1. As I said, the man is dead, and he was a scum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, when he spoke about Mr. Jekic, he said, quote, and this is at transcript 9696, line 1: "And what about Vojislav Jekic, the late Vojislav Jekic?" Were you aware, before Mr. Petrovic used the words "late Vojislav Jekic," that Mr. Jekic was dead?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I know he was killed in another shoot-out outside of a cafe in Belgrade. It isn't known who killed him, and to my knowledge, there was no indictment in that case either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 5874 be called to our screens. It is a media report issued the day after Mr. Jekic's death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, when the document is before you, would you please read it, and tell us whether you recognise the document as a report on what happened to Mr. Jekic. Do you recognise -- is this an accurate depiction of what you recall about the death of Mr. Jekic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. Could I object to the general nature of the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the question is superfluous, because it's clear what this is, Mr. Groome, isn't it? If you have any further questions on the document or if you -- not on the document, in relation to this, fine, but this is a report dated the 28th of April, 2006, and deals with the assassination of the ex-chief of the Loznica police, and names him as Vojislav Jekic. So, therefore, that seems to be clear, isn't it, unless there's any hidden message in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, there isn't, Your Honour. I simply would tender it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Objection, on the basis of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I suggest that -- do we need the witness to discuss this any further? Because I'm looking at the clock. You asked for 20 minutes. You've taken now 20 minutes. I said the Chamber would allow you to start. We'll need a break anyhow, because we are already 10 minutes over the usual 75 minutes. The Chamber may have some questions as well. We are less under a time pressure now, I understand, because I was informed, first of all, that the indirect flight which was obstructed by snow, that the snow has melted, or at least that the airport is open again which were to be used, and that if you are at -- that your flight departure is a little bit after 5.00. So, therefore, it seems that the practical problems do not put further pressure upon us. Mr. Groome, 20 minutes ago you said that you would need 20 minutes. How much more would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I count 12 questions, but it's often not easy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- I mean, the time pressure is gone, to some extent. I will also be generous if there is any further question by the Defence which -- Mr. Jordash, I -- if there are important matters which you have not raised because of time restraints, then I would be generous, but within the time-limits of today, and also within the time-limits of -- I think we said that we would stop at 1.30 today, and I'm not going to be blamed again for a late finish by those assisting us. Mr. Groome, let's be -- would 10 minutes do?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a portion of the tape of the original interview of the witness that I'd like to play for him. I don't know the precise time, and that's the real -- the unknown. I think we may be getting that information now. That tape, itself, Your Honour, is six minutes and twenty-four seconds. I imagine that would push me over 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I do not understand why you were unable to include this in your assessment 20 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As you see, Your Honour, I'm just getting the time now. We had problems with -- the copy that was in the system was unplayable. We had to re-digitise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that you provide us with the relevant portion of the transcript so that we can read it over the next half an hour or so?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have it here in court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you would take care that the Judges and the Defence will be provided with the relevant portion of the transcript, that might save some time. Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I also indicate, for Mr. Groome's purposes, that we also object to the reliability of this document. So that that could be addressed after the break, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you object to the reliability. Do you object against it being used or -- I don't know what questions Mr. Groome will have in relation to it, and, therefore, I'm a bit hesitant to say anything further about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, and, Your Honour, I was just indicating for Mr. Groome to consider that matter so I didn't ambush him with that objection later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm confused. Are we speaking about the media article or about the transcript from the original interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The media article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The media article?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry for the lack of clarification. Yes, it's the media article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The media article. We have plenty of time, isn't it, to discuss that? At this moment, the Chamber expects to receive the relevant portion of the transcript you'd like to use after the break, and you're invited to limit yourself to 10 minutes. And we'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, please proceed. You may be aware that the witness has been provided with a copy of the transcript as well in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The way I was going to suggest we proceed in that regard is, after I ask him about it -- was maybe just to play a few seconds to see if he recognises his own voice and then leave it for the Chamber to listen to it at another time, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any -- of course, if there's any dispute about the audio-recording being a forgery, that if the -- if not, then, of course, if you have time, please do so, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, before I ask you some questions on the portion of your interview -- your first interview, I want to finish up the topic of Mr. Jekic. Now, it's very clear to all of us in the courtroom your feelings for Mr. Jekic, and you've expressed them in very strong terms. This media report suggests that he was assassinated because he gave testimony before the courts of Serbia and, in that testimony, he identified the State Security Service as having a role in Arkan's murder. Can you give us one concrete -- or a concrete example of what Mr. Jekic did, that you have direct personal knowledge of, that leads you to have such strong feelings about his character?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact that he falsely represented himself, and we knew that in the Crisis Staff. Second, they would take money off people and promise to use their offices with certain functionaries in Belgrade in exchange for that. Whatever he did was outside the law, and the only thing he ever was involved in was wheeling and dealing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you say he falsely represented himself. I believe yesterday you said he represented himself as a member of State Security. What do you know about what organisation he worked for?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, in order to make sure that he wasn't falsely representing himself, we were with a delegate in Belgrade and I went to see Grujic, the president of the municipality. I took Grujic with me, and we went to the MUP of Serbia in Belgrade, to his office. We saw him seated in his office, along with four other colleagues. I told Grujic, Well, you can see very well, from the fact that he doesn't even have a telephone in his office, what sort of a position he has. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just so it doesn't become confused, are you saying you saw Mr. Jekic in a building in Belgrade that belonged to the MUP of Serbia; is that what your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you say that when you looked in the office, you did not see a telephone in the office; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw him sitting behind a desk in an office where six or seven more of his colleagues also had their desks. So when we came to see him, his boss recognised me. In fact, he was working for a service that was something like internal -- or in -- an inner control of the MUP. Since his boss hailed from Sabac, close to Zvornik, and I, therefore, knew him, he invited us to his office to have a cup of coffee with him. And in order to show in front of Grujic, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you some specific questions, and it's not necessary, the thing about the coffee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, there is no need for him to talk about sipping coffee. But, nevertheless, could he be allowed to finish what he was about to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- I think that he answered the question, and, therefore, Mr. Groome may intervene and put his next question to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, when you went up to the office, where you expected to see Mr. Jekic, were you allowed to go in without your identity being checked or were you required to identify yourself?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we reported to the reception desk and announced our visit. We said that we wanted to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'm a little confused, and maybe you can help me understand your evidence. If he's not the person who he's represented himself to be, how is it that he's sitting in the office where you expected to find him? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he introduced himself there an as employee of the State Security. Now, we went to the Public Security. He represented himself as the second or third person in importance in the MUP of Serbia, and I wanted to dissuade Grujic, who was the president of the municipality, of his impression that he, in fact, held the position he represented himself as having. I wanted to show that this wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand now. Now, the second reason you -- or basis for you having such strong feelings, you say he took money. Did he ever take money from you?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from me, but I know that he did take money from people I worked with -- or, rather, he took goods from a Zvornik factory that he never paid for, and also he took money from some people and he never paid them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there criminal complaints that we would be able to go and retrieve, in which we might learn more about these thefts by Mr. Jekic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certain that such documents exist. I cannot say exactly before which court, but I'm sure that there are many people that are involved in lawsuits with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, we will file the appropriate request. Now, I'd like to move to another topic, and this is your original interview. Over the break, you were provided a copy of the transcription of that interview in your own language. Can I ask you first: Did you have an opportunity to review the portion that you were provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my colleague, Mr. Groome, state clearly for which purposes he is going to use this part of the interview so that I would know what his intention was?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness take off his head-set?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take your earphones off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Jordash, in his examination, put to the witness that many of the details he provided in his evidence to the ICTY investigators was the result of seeing the Kula video - that's P61 in our case - numerous times. I simply want to establish in this document that there are a number of details here that are from the Kula video, yet I will establish that the Kula video, the first public viewing or display of the Kula video was one year later and it's a matter of public record in the Milosevic case, so to refute that particular assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, being informed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can understand that, but I would like to point out the fact that the Kula video is not the only source of possible information contained this paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course. But that's not what Mr. Groome says, but Mr. Groome wants to challenge the evidence that most of the details are coming from the Kula video. That's -- could you please -- Witness JF-026. Mr. Groome, please proceed. At the same time, to be quite clear, what is in the Kula video and what is said here, I think the parties could agree on what details do appear and do not appear, not -- we can ask the witness where he did get his details from, but not to compare the content of this with the Kula video, where we don't need the witness for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, JF-026, both Defence counsel are not contesting the authenticity of the tape of your original interview with investigators from the ICTY. But, nonetheless, I want to ask you: Having reviewed the transcript of that interview, do you recognise it as the first detailed interview you had with ICTY investigators?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe I've said the 65 ter number of this. This is 65 ter 5878. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the whole or just the excerpts we were provided with?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the excerpt, the audio excerpt, and the transcripts that you've been provided with, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's two pages, 17th of February, Day 2, Tape 69, pages 7 and 8. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after having read the transcript of that interview: Is it truthful, is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, yesterday Mr. Jordash -- do you believe that any information that's contained on that page that you reviewed is the result of you having seen the Kula video on public broadcast?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you said to Mr. Jordash that much of the detail you provided ICTY investigators was a result of seeing the Kula video, what details were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I look at the statement now, and if I compare it -- I don't know exactly which details you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. The information that's provided in that excerpt, is that a result of information that you possessed prior to seeing the Kula video or after seeing the Kula video?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even before I watched it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So everything in that excerpt you knew prior to having viewed the Kula video?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So then let me return to the question that Mr. Jordash asked you. What details -- what information did you provide the investigators that you did not possess prior to seeing the Kula video?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Some persons were mentioned, and I tried to recognise them. I'm not even sure whether I recognised all of them correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your answers to Mr. Jordash, you said -- with respect to whether you saw the Kula tape prior to giving your evidence, you said: "I'm not sure. I do not remember." I want to ask you to give additional thought to whether you saw the Kula tape prior to giving the first account of your evidence to ICTY investigators. It is a matter of public record that the first public showing of the Kula video occurred on the 19th of February, 2003, in the Milosevic trial, during the testimony of Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that Your Honours and my colleagues on the Defence can verify this: It occurred on Day 154 of the trial at transcript page 16440. The Prosecution informs the Trial Chamber that the Rule 70 provider of the tape has just authorised the public playing of the video. At transcript page 16451, Captain Dragan states that he first saw the Kula tape after arriving in The Hague. And, finally, at transcript page 16747, Captain Dragan states that on the evening of the day the tape was played, he called Frenki Simatovic and discussed Mr. Simatovic's reaction to what he heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the first public viewing of the tape was a full year after the interview that you gave to ICTY investigators. Do you -- has that refreshed your memory as to whether you relied on the Kula videotape for information provided the investigators?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did rely on that. I don't know when I first saw it. I really cannot recall now which period that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, at T-45, line 16, you said: "I have never seen them," referring to the two accused, "in my life before this, and so I was interested in seeing them. I saw Mr. Stanisic a few times in the newspapers." Now, after reading that portion of your initial interview with investigators, does that change your recollection as to whether you saw Mr. Stanisic prior to this courtroom here?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw him live. I saw him in the newspapers, and I saw this gentleman for the first time when the indictment was issued. I had not seen him even in the newspapers. I hadn't even heard of him, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I then ask you -- perhaps it's an error in the translation. You referred to the funeral of Radoslav -- Rade Kostic, and you say: "Jovica was there. I saw him then, for the first time then, in person." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise. You are right. I first saw Mr. Stanisic in person in 1995 at Kostic's funeral. I apologise. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there any other occasions that you saw him prior to coming into the court here?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the only time that I saw him in person, live, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you know what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I've concluded my examination, Your Honour. That saves some additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just cover quickly a couple of issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's -- perhaps, if you wouldn't mind, I have one or two questions for him, and often the Chamber is -- so in order to give an opportunity for you to consider the questions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-026 -- Witness JF-026, was -- Marko Pavlovic, was he involved in the arming of the population or volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he -- did he distribute the weapons through the Crisis Staff or through the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they come from JNA sources or are these included in the JNA weapons you told us about?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he participated in this transport from the Republic of the Serb Krajina and later on from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I have no further question for you. Mr. Jordash, Mr. Petrovic, who will go first? Mr. Petrovic, you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, two questions, and a remark, first of all. As for the time when this video was publicly played, I cannot challenge it. I have to check. I just know that the accused were shown this video considerably earlier. So that is one observation I wish to make. And now two questions, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the name of this boss of Jekic's who you went to see later, whose office you went to and who you talked to?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I know that the man was from Sabac, and he was an elderly man, about to retire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, briefly, what this boss of Jekic's said to you about Jekic.

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to know what he did, and I asked him -- in front of the president of the municipality, I said, What is this guy of ours doing, since he hails from Zvornik originally? And he said, He is basically a chicken thief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise someone else, perhaps, in this office that four or five persons were -- where four or five persons were sitting, in addition to Jekic?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have on the screen, please, 1D1642. And this is, again, a reference -- or a transcript of the same interview that Mr. Groome was referring to concerning the Red Berets, I think. The page that I want is two pages after the excerpt that Mr. Groome showed you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Jordash kindly speak into the other microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And on page 89 of e-court, page 10 of the interview, at line 13 of the transcript, it says -- the interviewer asks you the question: "When you say the Red Berets, what group are you referring to there?" You answer: "A special police group. "Q. Do you mean the group that had been in the news recently, the ones on the DB -- SDB, or are you referring to another group?" And you answer: "Yes, the one who was recently in news." What were you referring to has been in the news concerning the Red Berets at the point you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the context in which I was speaking at the time. What news?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the transcript appears to suggest you're speaking about a group called the Red Berets, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read the previous line to him, perhaps, where apparently the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the context is this: You're referring to military action in Divic, and you say this: "Okay --" Sorry, the Prosecutor asks you this: "Okay. Can you tell us, please, which units were involved in those operations and how those operations were carried out?" Your answer: "At that time, I was the director of Autotransport, and I don't know many details, but I know that the Red Berets took part and units of the Colonel Mico Stupar, special -- special forces from Pancevo. "Q. When you say the Red Berets, what group are you referring to there? "A. A special police group. "Q. Do you mean the group that had been in the news recently, the ones on the SDB, or are you referring to another group?" Answer -- you say this, Mr. Witness: "Yes, the one who was recently in news."

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of news are being referred to. But if it is the attack on Divici and Kula Grad, the Red Berets took part, the military ones belonging to Mr. Stupar, who then held the rank of lieutenant-colonel, because the military had some special unit that also wore red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But with reference to the news, are you able to say at this point what the news was that you'd watched and which the Prosecutor also appears to have watched?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember what kind of news that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's leave that there, then. Just one question, if I can, about Mr. Jekic. You say he represented himself as a member of the DB, and yet you didn't find that to be the case. Do you know what views he held towards the DB or to the accused, if any?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, really, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what his view was towards you?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was hostile, and I think that he had some kind of phobia to the effect that he wanted to become a member of the DB some day. So he had these bad relations with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he ever become a member of the DB, from what you know?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He ended up in Public Security. That's where he ended his career.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if he harboured hostile feelings towards the DB for not making that grade or employment?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, he did; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw it on the basis of his comments, that, in a way, he was kind of jealous. It seemed that he wanted to be that that he had introduced himself to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please allow me three questions that are based on the questions put by Mr. Jordash, very briefly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you remember something that was often called the rebellion of the Red Berets in Serbia in November 2001?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that all the newspapers, all the media, were writing and talking about it for days, who the Red Berets were, who was their founder, what their role was during the war and after the war?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the late prime minister of Serbia, Zoran Djindjic, went to Kula, to the centre of the Red Berets that had been named after Kostic, and that he negotiated with the Red Berets there?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that all the TV stations in Serbia broadcast Djindjic's conversations in Kula for days?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the minister of the interior, Mihajlovic, and the head of the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party in the Assembly of Serbia, Jovanovic, that they also went to Kula to talk to the members of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that for days, all the Serbian media reported about that, too?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These were five questions. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one line of question -- one question arising out of that last set of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you're the calling party, so that would open -- but I would certainly discourage you to put further questions within, of course, the framework of your duties. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-026, when Mr. Jordash asked you if you remembered what was in the news with respect to the Red Berets in November 2001 or around that time of your interview, you seemed to draw a complete blank. Yet when Mr. Petrovic has given you a really long list of very, very specific details 30 seconds later, you seem to have a recollection. How do you account for the change in recollection?

utterances.speaker: JF-026 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what Mr. Petrovic asked me is directly related to the assassination of the Serbian prime minister. That was repeated so many times, thousands of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, just a comment. You may or less blamed the witness in a change in recollection. I don't think, as a matter of fact, that that's the case. Mr. Jordash asked what he referred to at that time in the news he would have seen, and the questions after that by Mr. Petrovic, he asked for certain matters to be shown on television, not necessarily to be linked to what he said in his interview, although apparently you thought that that would be linked. But that was not established, at least not in the questions and the answers to it. No further questions? No. Witness JF-026, this concludes your testimony in this court. First of all, I'd like to thank you for coming. I'm also pleased by the fact that there's a fair chance that you might make it back home again today. There is, however, one matter still pending; that is, the extension of your protective measures. We, as you will remember, provisionally extended your protection to closed session, although reasons were not entirely clear yet. I would like to invite you to further explain, during the few -- time which remains, to further explain to the Victims and Witness Section what exactly your safety and security concerns are which you had not yet earlier explained to the Victims and Witness Section. And the Victims and Witness Section is invited to prepare a report on their discussions with you in relation to this. The Chamber will have to decide whether or not your testimony finally will be with the more limited protective measures, that is, face distortion, voice distortion and pseudonym, or whether it will remain confidential to the extent that it will be closed session evidence. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we'll adjourn in open session, if you would give me just one moment to check a few matters. Yes. One matter, briefly, Mr. Jordash. The witness was asked to review his testimony in the second case. No one has tendered it, nor have I heard a lot of questions about that. I'm not concerned about it, but that's the situation as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would like to tender it as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the other purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, as a Rule 92 ter document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you haven't asked him whether he had reviewed, whether there are any comments, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that's absolutely right, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to tender it under Rule 92 ter, you should at least provide for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I got so far yesterday and then the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then perhaps we -- let's see. Did you review the testimony you have given in the second case, the testimony that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you recognise this as the recording of your testimony given in January of this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you notice anything which you considered not to be truthful in that testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether that was because you find out later that it was not in accordance with the truth or whether it was by any mistake. So do I understand that if the same questions were put to you, that you would give substantially the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This matter has now been raised by me at this moment. Is there anything, but limited to this, which the parties would consider it necessary to ask the witness about? Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would only like to say that I stand by our position from the outset, which was that the witness -- the witness's evidence, what we heard in the courtroom, is the only thing that should be looked at. Various attestations of his previous statements and evidence I don't think can be very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a matter of weighing and evaluating the evidence. The only thing I was doing, where Mr. Jordash had not yet tendered the transcript and where he had not put any questions to the witness which might open the way to admission under Rule 92 ter, that at least we didn't let the witness go, because it might be difficult to repair it at any later stage. That's the only thing that we did at this moment. Any further discussion on admission or any further discussion on weighing or evaluating that evidence is not needed at this very moment. Then, Witness, we most likely will receive a report, then, from the Victims and Witness Section in which they reflect what you explained, as far as your security concerns are. This concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for staying with us for a couple of days. And I now invite the Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome, for next week, I think two witnesses are scheduled, Ewa Tabeau and another witness. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's what I wanted to raise with you. I expect by Tuesday, both will be here, both can testify, but I wonder whether it would be prudent, if everyone agrees, that we go straight to JF-029 and keep Ewa Tabeau again waiting on the shelf, as it were, so that she can be available to fill in a gap, should one arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know that we're in public session, so if you ask her to wait on the shelf --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against that? Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, this would pose a problem to us, in view of our preparations for these two witnesses. We followed the dynamics as they were announced to us, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please see whether you can find any agreement with Mr. Groome on this and see what's possible or not. If it's not possible, of course, the Chamber will have to decide on whether Mr. Groome is allowed to change the order of the appearance of the witnesses. Is there any other matter at this moment to be raised? If not, we will -- we adjourn, and we'll resume Tuesday, the 7th of December, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of December, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Closed session]    [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.40 p.m.,
